items.summary: Sigmund Freud (1856–1939) was an Austrian neurologist who founded psychoanalysis, a theory of the mind and a method for treating psychological disorders centered on the idea that unconscious mental processes shape thought and behavior. He developed influential concepts including the unconscious, repression, and the interpretation of dreams, and set them out in works such as The Interpretation of Dreams (1899/1900). His ideas were widely influential across psychology, psychiatry, and the humanities, including literary studies, while also drawing sustained scientific and philosophical criticism.

items.summary: Émile Durkheim (1858–1917) was a French sociologist widely regarded as one of the principal founders of sociology as an academic discipline. He argued that societies should be studied through "social facts" — ways of acting and thinking that are external to and coercive upon individuals — and applied this program in studies of the division of labor, suicide, and religion, set out in works such as The Rules of Sociological Method. His work also influenced anthropology, and he is commonly credited with helping to establish sociology's distinctive methods and subject matter.

source_hints.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Émile Durkheim

items.summary: Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) was a German philosopher and philologist whose work addressed morality, religion, culture, and the nature of value, developing themes such as the critique of traditional morality, the "will to power," and perspectivism. Writing in works including Thus Spoke Zarathustra and Beyond Good and Evil, he became one of the most influential figures in modern thought. He is commonly cited as a major influence on existentialism, continental philosophy, and critical theory, and his reception drew on and reacted against earlier thinkers such as Arthur Schopenhauer.

items.summary: Claude Lévi-Strauss (1908–2009) was a French anthropologist widely regarded as the founder of structural anthropology, an approach that analyzes culture — including myth, kinship, and classification — as systems of underlying structures modeled on the relational logic of structural linguistics. Drawing on the linguistics of Ferdinand de Saussure and Roman Jakobson, he set out this program in works such as The Elementary Structures of Kinship and Structural Anthropology. His methods were highly influential across the social sciences and the humanities, including literary theory.

source_hints.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Claude Lévi-Strauss

items.summary: Gottlob Frege (1848–1925) was a German logician, mathematician, and philosopher widely regarded as a founder of modern mathematical logic and analytic philosophy of language. In his Begriffsschrift (1879) he introduced a formal system of quantified logic that transformed the discipline, and he developed foundational analyses of concepts such as sense and reference. His work is commonly credited with helping to establish mathematical logic and the philosophy of language, and it influenced later work in linguistics.

items.summary: Alan Turing (1912–1954) was a British mathematician and logician widely regarded as a founder of computability theory and a pioneer of theoretical computer science. In his 1936 paper "On Computable Numbers," he introduced the abstract computing device now known as the Turing machine and used it to address the Entscheidungsproblem, establishing a formal notion of what it means for a function to be effectively computable. His ideas about machine intelligence, including the test later named after him, were also influential in the philosophy of mind.

items.summary: Charles Darwin (1809–1882) was a British naturalist widely regarded as the founder of evolutionary biology, best known for proposing that species evolve over generations through the process of natural selection. He set out this theory with extensive evidence in On the Origin of Species (1859), drawing on observations from his voyage on HMS Beagle and decades of subsequent study. His work reshaped the biological sciences and has also been cited as an influence on fields such as evolutionary psychology.

items.summary: Max Weber (1864–1920) was a German sociologist, historian, and political economist widely regarded as one of the founders of modern sociology. He is known for analyses of rationalization, authority, and bureaucracy, for his interpretive (verstehen) approach to social action, and for The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, which argued for a connection between certain religious ideas and the development of capitalism. His account of social and economic development is often contrasted with that of Karl Marx.

items.summary: Karl Marx (1818–1883) was a German philosopher, economist, and social theorist whose analysis of capitalism, class, and history has been widely influential across the social sciences, including sociology. In works such as Capital (Das Kapital), he analyzed the workings of capitalist production, value, and class relations, developing a materialist conception of history. His ideas are closely associated with the concept of false consciousness and gave rise to a broad tradition of Marxist thought in economics, politics, sociology, and philosophy.

items.summary: Edmund Husserl (1859–1938) was a German philosopher widely regarded as the founder of phenomenology, the philosophical study of the structures of consciousness and experience as they are given from a first-person point of view. Central to his work is the notion of intentionality — the directedness of consciousness toward objects — which he developed in works such as Logical Investigations and Ideas. His phenomenological method influenced later philosophy, including existentialism and, more broadly, the philosophy of cognitive science.

items.summary: Noam Chomsky is an American linguist and cognitive scientist widely credited with founding generative grammar, an approach that treats a language's grammar as a finite system of explicit rules generating its grammatical sentences and as a representation of speakers' tacit linguistic knowledge. His work introduced the influential hypothesis of an innate universal grammar and helped shift linguistics and cognitive science toward the study of the mind, contributing to the mid-twentieth-century "cognitive revolution." He is also widely known as a public intellectual.

items.summary: Donald Knuth is an American computer scientist widely credited with helping to establish the analysis of algorithms as a rigorous area of computer science, principally through his multi-volume work The Art of Computer Programming. He is also known for creating the TeX typesetting system and for foundational contributions to the theory and mathematical analysis of algorithms. His work is commonly regarded as central to the development of computer science as a mathematical discipline.

items.summary: On the Origin of Species is an 1859 book by Charles Darwin that presents the theory of evolution by natural selection, arguing that species descend with modification from common ancestors and that natural selection is a principal mechanism driving this change. Marshalling extensive evidence from natural history, breeding, and biogeography, it is widely regarded as one of the foundational and most influential works of modern biology and as the canonical text establishing evolutionary biology.

items.summary: Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica ("Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy"), commonly called the Principia, is a work by Isaac Newton first published in 1687 that sets out his laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation. Written in Latin and using geometrical methods, it provides a unified mathematical account of terrestrial and celestial motion and is widely regarded as one of the most important works in the history of science and a foundational text of classical physics.

items.summary: The Wealth of Nations, full title An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, is a 1776 work by the Scottish philosopher and economist Adam Smith. It analyzes how national wealth arises from the division of labor, productive labor, and markets coordinated through self-interested exchange, and argues broadly in favor of free trade and limited government intervention. It is widely regarded as a foundational text of modern economics and as the canonical work marking the emergence of the discipline as a systematic field of study.

items.summary: Cours de linguistique générale ("Course in General Linguistics") is a foundational work of modern linguistics, compiled by students from lecture notes and published in 1916, after his death, under the name of the Swiss linguist Ferdinand de Saussure. It sets out key distinctions such as langue and parole, the synchronic and diachronic study of language, and the arbitrary nature of the linguistic sign, treating language as a system of signs. It is widely regarded as a founding text of structural linguistics and a major influence on structuralism across the humanities.

items.summary: "A Mathematical Theory of Communication" is a 1948 paper by Claude Shannon, published in the Bell System Technical Journal, that founded the field of information theory. It introduced a quantitative measure of information (entropy), the modeling of communication sources and channels, and results on the fundamental limits of data compression and reliable transmission over noisy channels. It is widely regarded as the canonical work establishing information theory and is foundational to modern communications, computing, and data science.

items.summary: The Interpretation of Dreams (German: Die Traumdeutung) is a book by Sigmund Freud, published in 1899 and dated 1900, that presents his theory that dreams are disguised fulfillments of unconscious wishes and can be analyzed to reveal repressed mental content. It introduces influential concepts such as the distinction between the manifest and latent content of dreams and the mechanisms of dream-work, and lays out central ideas of psychoanalysis. It is widely regarded as one of Freud's foundational works and a canonical text of psychoanalysis.

items.summary: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus is a philosophical work by Ludwig Wittgenstein, first published in German in 1921 and in English translation in 1922. Written as a series of numbered propositions, it advances a picture theory of meaning and analyzes the relationship between language, thought, and the world, culminating in claims about the limits of what can be meaningfully said. It is widely regarded as a major work of analytic philosophy and a canonical text in the philosophy of language and logic.

items.summary: Capital, Volume I (German: Das Kapital, Volume I) is an 1867 work of political economy by Karl Marx, the first and only volume he published in his lifetime; the later volumes were edited from his manuscripts and published after his death. It presents a critical analysis of capitalist production, developing Marx's account of the commodity, value, and the extraction of surplus value from labor. It is widely regarded as a foundational text of Marxist thought and has been highly influential across economics and the social sciences, including sociology.

items.summary: "On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem" is a 1936 paper by Alan Turing that introduces the abstract computing device now known as the Turing machine and defines the notion of a computable number. Using this framework, Turing showed that certain problems, including the decision problem (Entscheidungsproblem) for first-order logic, cannot be solved by any such machine. It is widely regarded as a founding paper of computability theory and theoretical computer science.

items.summary: Natural selection is the process by which heritable traits that improve an organism's chances of survival and reproduction tend to become more common in a population over successive generations, while less advantageous traits become rarer. It was proposed as a principal mechanism of evolution by Charles Darwin (and independently by Alfred Russel Wallace) in the mid-nineteenth century and set out in detail in On the Origin of Species (1859). It is a central concept of evolutionary biology and, together with other mechanisms, accounts for the adaptation and diversification of living things.

items.summary: In psychoanalysis, the unconscious is the part of the mind comprising mental processes — such as wishes, memories, and drives — that are not accessible to conscious awareness but are held to influence thought, emotion, and behavior. The concept was central to the psychoanalytic theory developed by Sigmund Freud, who held that unconscious material is kept from awareness by repression and can be inferred through phenomena such as dreams and slips. It is a foundational idea of psychoanalysis, though the notion of unconscious mental processes has a longer history and is understood differently across later psychology.

items.summary: A Turing machine is an abstract model of computation, introduced by Alan Turing in 1936, consisting of an infinite tape, a read/write head, and a finite set of states and rules that determine its behavior. Despite its simplicity, it can capture the notion of any effectively computable procedure, and it is used to make precise what it means for a function to be computable and for a problem to be decidable. It is a foundational concept of computability theory and theoretical computer science, closely associated with the Church–Turing thesis.

items.summary: A Nash equilibrium is a solution concept in game theory describing a set of strategies, one for each player, such that no player can improve their outcome by unilaterally changing strategy while the others keep theirs fixed. It was introduced by the mathematician John Nash in the early 1950s, who proved that such an equilibrium exists in a broad class of games. It is a central concept of non-cooperative game theory and is widely applied in economics, political science, and other fields that model strategic interaction.

items.summary: Mendelian inheritance is the set of principles describing how discrete hereditary units — now identified with genes — are passed from parents to offspring, including the segregation of paired factors during reproduction and the independent assortment of different factors. These principles derive from the mid-nineteenth-century experiments of Gregor Mendel on pea plants, whose work was rediscovered around 1900 and became foundational to the science of genetics. Mendelian inheritance forms the classical basis of genetics, later extended and refined by the discovery of chromosomes, linkage, and molecular genetics.

items.summary: A social fact is a concept introduced by the sociologist Émile Durkheim to denote ways of acting, thinking, and feeling that are external to individuals and exert a coercive influence over them, such as laws, customs, moral rules, and institutions. Durkheim argued that social facts are the proper subject matter of sociology and should be studied objectively, "as things," rather than reduced to individual psychology. The concept is foundational to sociology and to Durkheim's program for establishing it as an autonomous science.

items.summary: The "invisible hand" is a metaphor associated with the economist Adam Smith, used to describe how individuals pursuing their own self-interest in a market can unintentionally promote outcomes that benefit society as a whole. Smith used the phrase sparingly in his writings, including The Wealth of Nations, and it has since become a widely cited shorthand in economics for the idea that decentralized, self-interested exchange can produce socially beneficial coordination without central direction. It remains a foundational and much-discussed concept in economics, subject to varied interpretation.

items.summary: In philosophy, intentionality is the property of mental states of being about, directed at, or representing objects or states of affairs. The term in its modern sense was reintroduced by Franz Brentano, who treated directedness toward an object as the mark of the mental, and it was central to the phenomenology developed by Edmund Husserl, who made the analysis of intentional consciousness a core part of his method. Intentionality is a central topic in phenomenology and the philosophy of mind, where it figures in debates about mental representation and consciousness.

items.summary: The lambda calculus is a formal system for expressing computation based on function abstraction and application, introduced by the logician Alonzo Church in the 1930s. Using a small set of rules for defining and applying functions, it provides a universal model of computation equivalent in power to the Turing machine, a correspondence expressed in the Church–Turing thesis. It is a foundational concept in computability theory and in the theory of programming languages, where it underlies functional programming.

items.summary: Symbolic artificial intelligence is an approach to AI that represents knowledge using explicit symbols and rules and performs reasoning by manipulating these symbolic representations, for example through logic, search, and rule-based systems. It was the dominant paradigm of AI research from the mid-twentieth century into the 1980s, associated with early figures of the field such as those at the founding Dartmouth workshop, and includes expert systems and logic-based reasoning. It is often contrasted with connectionist and statistical machine-learning approaches, and remains a recognized subfield of artificial intelligence.

items.summary: False consciousness is a concept in the Marxist tradition referring to a systematically mistaken understanding of one's true social and economic situation, especially the way in which members of a subordinate class may hold beliefs that serve the interests of a dominant class rather than their own. Although the specific term is generally attributed to Friedrich Engels rather than to Karl Marx himself, it is closely associated with Marx's account of ideology and class, and it was developed by later Marxist theorists. It remains a discussed concept in sociology and social and political theory.
